deep.reconstruction:
Context: this page opens the main text of Riemann's fragment 'Zwei allgemeine Sätze über lineare Differentialgleichungen mit algebraischen Coefficienten' (1857, printed posthumously in the Werke, 1876). It sets up the monodromy data of a system of n functions and proves the global relation among the local monodromies.

(1) Setting. Let y = (y_1,...,y_n) be functions of x. They are single-valued (the MS word is probably 'einwerthig') and finite on the whole x-sphere except at the branch points a,b,c,...,g. Analytic continuation of x once around a branch point carries y into constant linear combinations of its former values.

(2) Normalization. Draw a closed Jordan curve through all branch points in the order a,b,...,g. It splits the sphere into two simply connected regions, in each of which the y's are single-valued and continuous. The values on the positive side are taken as the given branches.

(3) Local monodromy. A positive loop around a sends y_nu to sum_i A_i^(nu) y_i, nu=1..n. Similarly B_i^(nu) for b, ..., G_i^(nu) for g. In modern terms: y -> A y, where A = (A_i^nu) has row index nu and column index i. So (A)(y) denotes the column vector A·y.

(4) Relation. Riemann states (G)(F)...(B)(A) = (0), where (0) is the identity substitution (defined on the next page).

The proof is on the next page; restated here. Let x run along the boundary curve. Between consecutive branch points it stays on the positive side, and at each branch point it makes a positive half-turn around it. Then y becomes successively (A)(y), (B)(A)(y), ..., (G)(F)...(B)(A)(y).

The same path is homotopic to running around the whole boundary of the negative region. There the functions are single-valued, so y must return to its original values. Hence the composite substitution is the identity.

Modern form: the product of the local monodromies around all singular points, taken in the cyclic order fixed by the cut, is the identity. Equivalently, the monodromy representation of pi_1(P^1 minus {a,...,g}) is generated by loops gamma_a,...,gamma_g with gamma_a...gamma_g = 1. (Remark mine: the point at infinity must be counted among a..g if it is singular.)

On composition order (mine): (B)(A) is to be read as composition of substitutions, 'first A, then B'. As matrix products acting on the column y, continuing first around a and then around b gives A·(B·y). So Riemann's (G)...(B)(A) corresponds to the matrix product A·B·...·G = I. This anti-homomorphism is the classical convention. The condition is the same up to inversion and reversal of the order, and is self-consistent.
errors: No mathematical error. The proof (on the next page) implicitly uses that the boundary path is contractible within the closure of the negative region. It also needs infinity either counted among the branch points or regular; Riemann covers this by 'für alle complexen Werthe'.

The meaning of the juxtaposition (B)(A) is not made explicit. As a literal matrix product acting on column vectors, the correct relation is A·B·...·G = I, not G·...·B·A = I. Read as composition of substitutions 'first (A), then (B)', Riemann's formula is correct. This is a notational subtlety, not an error.
The equation is written '= (0)', with (0) used for the identity substitution. This is unconventional notation, explained on the next page.

results.what: Description of a system of n multivalued functions by constant linear substitutions (monodromy matrices) around branch points, after fixing branches by a closed cut through all singular points
results.modern_name: Monodromy representation / local system on the punctured sphere
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann (1857 Abel-type memoir on the hypergeometric function P-function; this 1857 fragment, published 1876)

results.what: Product of all local monodromy matrices in cyclic order equals the identity
results.modern_name: Relation gamma_1...gamma_k = 1 in pi_1 of the punctured sphere (global monodromy relation)
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann (this fragment, Werke 1876); standard in Riemann–Hilbert problem literature

deep.surprise_reason: This is the opening of Riemann's well-known 1857 fragment on linear ODEs with algebraic coefficients. It was printed in the Werke (1876) and is the classical origin of the monodromy/Riemann–Hilbert problem. The content is known and credited to him.

checkable.asserts: Scalar example (n=1): y=(x-a)^al (x-b)^(-al) is single-valued at infinity. Its monodromies exp(2*pi*I*al) at a and exp(-2*pi*I*al) at b multiply to 1.
Given any two local monodromies, the third (around the remaining point) is determined by the relation A*B*C = I. This illustrates the constraint that the relation imposes on the class of systems.
Substituting y -> B y into the components of A y gives A*B*y. So 'first A, then B' corresponds to the matrix product A*B (anti-homomorphism convention).

transcription_corrections: The final equation in the image reads '(G)(F) ... (B)(A) = (0)', not '= (1)'. The next page explains (0) as the identity substitution; '(1)' there is the equation's number.
'einändrig' is almost certainly 'einwerthig' (single-valued), consistent with 'einwerthig' on the next page.
'theile man' is more likely 'scheide man' in the image ('Zu ihrer näheren Bestimmung scheide man die Gesammtheit ...').
The struck-out character before 'mittelst' is a deleted fragment (shown as [-d-]); the reading 'die aus (y) mittelst des Coefficientensystems (A) gebildeten Werthe' is otherwise correct.
